name: Diced cartilage in fascia (DCF)

lead: Diced cartilage in fascia (DCF) is a nose surgery technique in which cartilage, often taken from the rib, is cut into small pieces and wrapped in a sleeve of fascia. The wrapped graft is placed along the bridge of the nose to raise it or smooth irregularities.
The appearance payoff is a higher, straighter and smoother nasal dorsum, including in noses over-reduced by earlier surgery or with a saddle deformity.

paras: A surgeon harvests cartilage and fascia, dices the cartilage and wraps it in the fascia, then places the graft in a pocket on the nasal dorsum. It is used in primary and revision rhinoplasty, in post-trauma reconstruction and in feminising rhinoplasty. Recovery follows standard nasal surgery routines under a surgeon's guidance.

As with any surgery, risks include complications at the nose and at the graft donor site, and results depend on healing. Published series report both functional and aesthetic gains and note complications are possible; a surgeon can explain individual risk.

angle.text: DCF directly builds volume along the bridge of the nose. Surgeons use it to raise a low or saddled dorsum and to fix irregularities after earlier surgery.

lead: Diced cartilage in fascia (DCF) is a technique for building up the nasal dorsum. Cartilage is cut into small pieces and wrapped in fascia, forming a malleable graft that is shaped on the nose. It was developed to counteract the warping, visibility and displacement of solid rib cartilage grafts.[1]

A randomised trial of 36 patients needing major dorsal augmentation compared two fascial wraps for diced rib cartilage; wrapping with rectus muscle fascia from the rib harvest site produced shorter operating times, higher satisfaction and shorter hospital stays than deep temporal fascia.[1]

DCF is reported across many settings: Asian augmentation rhinoplasty, over-resected noses, saddle nose reconstruction, Le Fort II fracture repair and feminising rhinoplasty in transgender patients.[2][3][4][5][6]
infobox: Diced cartilage (often costal) wrapped in fascia

paras: Rib cartilage is an abundant donor source for significant dorsal augmentation, and wrapping the diced pieces in fascia is intended to reduce warping, visibility and displacement compared with solid grafts.[1] The wrapping technique has evolved over time, and variants include a version wrapped in oxidised cellulose (the Turkish Delight technique described by Erol in 2000) and a case report using periprosthetic capsule as the wrap.[7]

Reviews describe diced cartilage grafting within Asian augmentation rhinoplasty and in correcting over-resected noses.[2][3] It has also been reported in feminising rhinoplasty and in simultaneous repair of Le Fort II fractures with rhinoplasty.[5][6]

The 2014 randomised trial of 36 patients found rectus fascia wraps gave shorter operating times, higher satisfaction and shorter stays than temporal fascia wraps.[1] A prospective study in Yemen of 30 patients with saddle nose deformity reported the A-B line measurement rose from 16.75 mm to 21 mm and the NOSE score improved from 52.8 to 5, with high satisfaction.[4] Case series and case reports describe use in Le Fort II reconstruction and in capsule-wrapped variants.[6][7]
